newsitem.title: UK: British union conference could rock Labour boat.
newsitem.headline: British union conference could rock Labour boat.

text.p: Britain's trade unions hold their annual conference in the seaside town of Blackpool next week, with most union leaders -- and the Labour Party -- hoping no one will make waves before elections due within eight months.

Labour has cut union influence over its policies and moved to the centre under leader Tony Blair, but the unions that still provide much of its funds are closely linked with Labour in the public mind, and party bosses see that as a liability.
As every year, the leadership of the Trades Union Congress (TUC) confederation -- not itself affiliated to Labour -- is desperately trying to take the spotlight off party politics.
"I'm much more concerned about relations with the government than with the Labour Party," TUC general secretary John Monks told a news conference called to discuss the agenda.

All the same, the liveliest debate of the week is likely to come next Wednesday when some unions will put pressure on Labour to fix a national minimum wage quickly if it wins the election. The TUC leadership will not be asking the conference to back a precise figure, but left-wing unions, including the National Union of Mineworkers led by Arthur Scargill, are backing a motion calling for Labour to introduce a legal minimum wage of 4.26 pounds ($6.68) an hour within a year of taking office.

"That sounds like a recruiting slogan for Socialist Labour rather than anything that's got much to do with negotiations with the government," John Edmonds, leader of the big general union, the GMB, said in an interview this week.
The Socialist Labour Party was set up by Scargill in May after he quit Labour in disgust at its centrist turn.

Monks told the news conference the TUC's general council, made up of himself and leaders of member unions, felt a minimum of four pounds would be "reasonable", but it would not back any precise figure until real negotiations were about to start.
The Labour Party is committed to introducing a minimum wage, but it, too, has declined to name a figure. It will set up a commission including unions and employers to recommend a level.

TUC leaders persuaded members not to fix a precise figure at last year's conference, to avoid giving ammunition to Labour's opponents, but they said then they would set a level this time around and campaign for it ahead of the next election.

However, Monks told the news conference that the debate was "hypothetical" without a Labour government, adding the TUC would set a figure "when we're clear about the timetable for a Low Pay Commission and if there is going to be a Low Pay Commission".

Blair has promised to give employees and unions more rights within the workplace, but he has refused to repeal all the anti-union laws brought in by the right-wing Conservatives who have been in power since 1979. An angry debate on this is likely on Thursday.
He has upset many union leaders by backtracking on a 1993 promise made by his predecessor, the late John Smith, to give workers full rights from their first day with an employer.
"It seems to me outrageous that you can say, for a period of time people can be dismissed unfairly. That doesn't seem to be quite the standards of a civilised country," Edmonds said.
The TUC's stand on the European single currency will also come in for criticism from some left-wing unions.

The TUC believes that if European economic and monetary union goes ahead, it would be better for Britain to be part of it than left outside. But some unionists are worried about the deflationary budgetary policies required of prospective members trying to meet the economic criteria they must meet before joining. ($1=.6373 Pound)
